readingInstruction: Read 2 Chronicles 17:1-20:37. Jehoshaphat sends teachers throughout Judah, makes an unwise alliance with Ahab, and then, when a vast army comes, leads the nation in prayer. Read 20:1-30 closely.
settingTheScene: Jehoshaphat is one of the Chronicler’s favorite kings. He sends officials, Levites, and priests with the Book of the Law to teach in every city of Judah. He appoints judges. But he also allies himself with the wicked Ahab. When Moab, Ammon, and others come against him, he proclaims a fast and leads Judah in a great prayer. The result is one of the most remarkable victories in Scripture.
observation: “And they taught in Judah, having the Book of the Law of the LORD with them” (17:9).
“Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD?” (19:2).
“Consider what you do, for you judge not for man but for the LORD” (19:6).
“Then Jehoshaphat was afraid and set his face to seek the LORD, and proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah” (20:3).
“O our God, will you not execute judgment on them? For we are powerless against this great horde that is coming against us. We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you” (20:12).
“Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed at this great horde, for the battle is not yours but God’s” (20:15).
“Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be established; believe his prophets, and you will succeed” (20:20).
“And when they began to sing and praise, the LORD set an ambush against the men of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir” (20:22).
interpretation:
Jehoshaphat’s best moment is when he sends teachers. Notice the method: officials, Levites, and priests go through the cities “having the Book of the Law of the LORD with them.” Spiritual health comes through teaching God’s word. The result was that the fear of the LORD fell on neighboring kingdoms, and they did not make war against Judah.

His worst moment is his alliance with Ahab. The prophet Micaiah is the one true voice against four hundred false prophets, and Jehoshaphat sees the king of Israel struck and nearly dies himself. The prophet Jehu asks, “Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD?” But he adds that there is some good in him. God’s grace works in people with mixed records.

Then the great crisis arrives. A vast army comes from beyond the Dead Sea. The king is afraid, and the fear drives him to God, not away from him. He gathers the whole nation, including “their little ones, their wives, and their children,” and prays. His prayer begins with who God is, “You rule over all the kingdoms of the nations,” recalls God’s promises about the temple, and then admits the truth: “We are powerless… We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you.” That sentence is one of the best prayers a person can pray.

God answers through a Levite named Jahaziel: “The battle is not yours but God’s.” The next morning, Jehoshaphat appoints singers to go before the army, praising “for his steadfast love endures forever.” When they began to sing, God set ambushes, and the enemy destroyed each other. Judah collected plunder for three days and gathered in the Valley of Beracah, “blessing.” The nation returned to Jerusalem with harps, lyres, and trumpets.
connection: Ephesians 6:12: we do not wrestle against flesh and blood. Romans 8:31: if God is for us, who can be against us? 2 Corinthians 4:8: “We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed… perplexed, but not driven to despair.” Acts 16:25-26 shows Paul and Silas singing in prison. 1 Samuel 17:47: “The battle is the LORD’s.” Isaiah 26:3: you keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you.
application:
Use Jehoshaphat’s prayer the next time you face something beyond you: “I do not know what to do, but my eyes are on you.”

Try praising God in the middle of a hard situation, before you see the answer.

Be careful with your closest alliances, and ask whether they pull you toward or away from God.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you cannot manage, and say, “My eyes are on you.”
Thank him that the battle is his.
Ask him to teach you to worship before you see the victory.
